title: Time of day and the week
teaches: How the trading day and week are shaped: heavy volume and wide spreads at the open, a quiet midday, the closing auction at 4:00 p.m. with its 3:50 p.m. imbalances and cutoffs, the holidays and index rebalances on the calendar, and why old weekday folklore has faded.

walkthroughs.title: The shape of a day
steps: Volume runs heavy near the open, slows at midday, then builds again into the close.
The open prices in a whole night of news. It tends to swing hardest, and spreads are usually widest.
The day ends in the closing auction, often one of the day's biggest single trades.

walkthroughs.title: The last ten minutes
steps: From 3:50 p.m., NYSE and Nasdaq publish the closing imbalance: on-close shares left unmatched, and on which side.
3:50 p.m. is also NYSE's cutoff for new market-on-close orders. Nasdaq takes them until 3:55 p.m.
At 4:00 p.m. the closing auction runs. On Nasdaq, it sets the official closing price.
Some of our setups, like the Slingshot and the Launchpad, enter on the close. This is when they act.

walkthroughs.title: Next week, from Sunday
steps: On Sunday, map the week: holidays and early closes, earnings dates, the Fed and the big data days.
Some Friday closes are giant. The Russell indexes now rebalance every June and December, and index funds trade that close.
Friday's close starts two days without a regular session. Weekend news can gap the stock at Monday's open.
Old weekday rules, like weak Mondays, have faded since they were published. Plan around real dates.

questions.q: On a normal day, when do the most shares trade?
choices: Near the open and near the close
About evenly all day long
Mostly in the middle of the day
Mostly in the hours after close
questions.answer: Near the open and near the close
questions.why: Near the open and near the close. Volume is usually heavy early, slows at midday, and builds again into the close. This is a tendency, and exceptions can happen any day. After the close, trading interest drops, and spreads usually widen.
questions.lesson_line: Busy early, quiet midday, busy late. The trading day has a shape.

wrong.About evenly all day long: Volume isn't flat. Broker research and academic work both describe it bunching up around the open and the close.
wrong.Mostly in the middle of the day: Midday is the quiet stretch. The action slows there, then picks up again late.
wrong.Mostly in the hours after close: After the close, trading interest drops. Extended hours usually bring wider spreads, or no quote at all.

questions.simple: Most shares usually trade near the open and near the close, while the middle of the day tends to be quiet.

reasons: Schwab and Investopedia are not fully independent (conflicts); Hong and Wang backs the shape

questions.q: Trading by the day of the week tends to give you an edge.
questions.why: False. Trading by the day of the week gains nothing, all else equal. In S&P 500 data, every weekday is up on 52% to 54% of days. Old research found weak Mondays, but the weekend effect seems to have weakened or disappeared once published.
questions.lesson_line: Weekday folklore isn't a plan. Trade the setup, not the day of the week.
questions.simple: False. The weekday alone gains you nothing, since every weekday is up on about the same share of days.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: On a typical day, bid-ask spreads are widest right at the ___.
questions.why: Open. The spread is the gap between the bid, the most a buyer pays, and the ask, the least a seller takes. Cboe data on large US stocks show spreads widest at the open, then narrowing toward the close. For you, the first minutes cost the most to trade, since you buy at the ask and sell at the bid.
questions.lesson_line: The first minutes are usually the priciest to trade. Wide spreads come with the open.
questions.simple: The open. Spreads are widest in the first minutes, so that is often the priciest time to trade.

reasons: two Tier 2 publishers agree (Cboe, Journal of Finance)

questions.q: Why does the open often swing harder than the rest of the day?
choices: It prices in news since the close
Earnings come out right at 9:30 a.m.
Spreads are tightest at the open
Big funds do most of their trading then
questions.answer: It prices in news since the close
questions.why: It prices in the news since the last close. The 9:30 a.m. open takes in everything that broke overnight at once. News outside trading hours can unbalance buy and sell orders. Then a stock can open far from the prior close. That is why the open often swings hardest.
questions.lesson_line: The open settles a whole night of news. Expect it to swing.

Companies usually report before the open or after the close, not at the bell. The open reacts to news that's already out.
wrong.Spreads are tightest at the open: The other way round. Spreads are typically widest at the open and narrow through the day.
wrong.Big funds do most of their trading then: Our sources put a lot of institutional trading late in the day, not mostly at the open. The open's swing comes from the news since the close.

questions.simple: The open swings more because it has to take in all the news since the last close at once.

reasons: Investopedia and Schwab agree; stable idea

questions.q: The 4:00 p.m. closing auction is often one of the day's biggest trades.
questions.why: True. The opening and closing auction prints are typically the day's largest single trades. NYSE calls its closing auction the largest single liquidity event in US equities trading. In Q2 2024, US closing auctions matched $55.5 billion a day, a record. It is typical, not a promise for every stock on every day.
questions.lesson_line: A big slice of the day can trade in one print at 4:00 p.m.
questions.simple: True, because the closing auction often holds one of the biggest single trades of the whole day.

reasons: dated numbers that change (Q2 2024 auction totals)

questions.q: On a normal day, who does a lot of trading near the close, and why?
choices: Index funds, to match their benchmark
Companies, to report earnings at 4:00
Day traders, to open overnight trades
Fed watchers, to react to 2:00 news
questions.answer: Index funds, to match their benchmark
questions.why: Index funds, to match their benchmark. Index-fund managers generally trade near the close. Institutions may do a lot of their trading late in the day too. On a Russell rebalance Friday the flow is huge: $219.9 billion traded in the closing moments on NYSE in June 2026.
questions.lesson_line: Money that tracks an index tends to trade the close. That's part of why the last minutes get busy.

wrong.Companies, to report earnings at 4:00: Companies usually report before the open or after the close, and a report isn't a trade.
wrong.Day traders, to open overnight trades: Day traders close out late in the day. The last hour sees them closing positions, not opening overnight ones.
wrong.Fed watchers, to react to 2:00 news: A normal day has no Fed statement. One comes after a Fed meeting: on Oct. 28, 2026, it came out at 2:00 p.m. Index-fund managers generally trade near the close.

questions.simple: Index funds trade near the close, because they want to match the index they track.

reasons: the key rests on one publisher (Schwab f44, f45), unreachable on 2026-11-12

questions.q: Midday is usually the quietest stretch of the trading day.
questions.why: True. Volume and volatility often fade by late morning. The middle of the day tends to be the calmest part of the session.
questions.lesson_line: Midday is usually the slow part of the day. Expect less volume and smaller moves.

questions.q: The first half hour is usually the calmest part of the trading day.
questions.why: False. A study of actively traded stocks found volume and volatility higher in the first half hour. The open tends to be one of the most volatile, active times of the day. The calm stretch is usually the middle of the day, not the start.
questions.lesson_line: The first 30 minutes are usually one of the wildest stretches of the day, not the calmest.
questions.simple: False, because the first half hour is usually one of the busiest and wildest parts of the day.

questions.q: What starts at 3:50 p.m. on both NYSE and Nasdaq?
choices: Closing imbalance info goes out
The regular session ends
After-hours trading begins
Market orders stop being taken
questions.why: Closing imbalance info goes out. From 3:50 p.m., NYSE and Nasdaq publish the on-close shares that would be left unmatched. NYSE also stops taking new market-on-close and limit-on-close orders then, except on the side that offsets a significant imbalance. Regular orders, market orders included, keep working until 4:00 p.m. Nasdaq takes market-on-close orders until 3:55 p.m.
questions.lesson_line: From 3:50 p.m. the exchanges show which side is heavy into the close. The last ten minutes get busy.

wrong.After-hours trading begins: The regular session runs to 4:00 p.m. After-hours trading comes after that.
wrong.Market orders stop being taken: Regular orders, market orders included, keep working until 4:00 p.m. The 3:50 changes are about on-close orders, and Nasdaq takes market-on-close orders until 3:55.
wrong.The regular session ends: That's 4:00 p.m., when the closing auction runs. Regular trading goes on until then.

questions.simple: At 3:50 p.m. both exchanges start showing the closing imbalance, the shares left without a match.

reasons: exchange times and cutoffs can change

questions.q: Sunday night, you plan the week ahead. What goes on your checklist?
choices: Holidays, early closes, earnings
Which weekday is up the most often
Last week's best time to buy
Fed and CPI days, so you can sit out
questions.why: Holidays, early closes and earnings. They are dated, and they change what you can do. A holiday or a 1:00 p.m. close moves any plan that acts on the close. Companies usually report before the open or after the close. Our rule: no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. Fed and CPI days are not a reason to sit out: we trade them like any other day.
questions.lesson_line: Plan around real dates. Holidays, early closes and earnings dates shape the week.

wrong.Which weekday is up the most often: Weekdays barely differ. In S&P 500 data each one is up on 52% to 54% of days.
wrong.Last week's best time to buy: Intraday tendencies are averages, not a schedule. Exceptions happen any day, and big news like a Fed announcement can upset them.
wrong.Fed and CPI days, so you can sit out: That's a news-day rule, and we don't have one. We trade Fed and CPI days like any other day.

questions.simple: Map holidays, early closes and earnings dates, because they change what your plans can do that week.

questions.q: Thin stock. 9:31: $24.80 bid, $25.10 ask. 10:30: $24.98 bid, $25.02 ask. Buy 1,000 at the ask, sell at the bid. Extra cost at 9:31 vs 10:30?
questions.why: Buy at the ask and sell at the bid, and you give up the whole spread on every share. On 1,000 shares the 9:31 spread costs $300 and the 10:30 spread costs $40. The extra cost at 9:31 is the gap, $260. Spreads are typically widest at the open.
questions.lesson_line: In a thin stock, the first minutes can be the priciest time to trade. Check the spread first.
questions.simple: It costs $260 more, because the 9:31 spread is far wider than the 10:30 one on 1,000 shares.

wrong.$300: Only the 9:31 cost. Subtract the 10:30 cost to get the extra.
wrong.$340: Added the two spreads. The extra cost is their difference.

questions.story: Day one of a Kicker. At 9:42 a.m. it's already well up from the open. You missed the first entry, over the red day's high.
questions.q: What's our plan's other way in today?
choices: A break of the opening range high
Buy now, before it runs further
Buy the close, once the day is done
Wait for a quiet dip near midday
questions.answer: A break of the opening range high
questions.why: A break of the 30-minute opening range. That is our Kicker plan's second day-one entry. The first is over the red day's high, at market as it trades through. Let the first 30 minutes set the range, then act on the break. Both entries trigger during the Kicker day, not on the close.
questions.lesson_line: Let the first 30 minutes draw the range. Then trade the break, not the noise inside it.

wrong.Buy now, before it runs further: At 9:42 the 30-minute range isn't set yet, so there is nothing to break. The first entry has passed, and neither entry says buy now.
wrong.Buy the close, once the day is done: Every setup buys as price trades through its trigger, during the day, never at the close. Both Kicker entries trigger during the day.
wrong.Wait for a quiet dip near midday: A dip isn't in the plan. The trigger is the break of the opening range, whenever it comes.

questions.simple: Wait for the stock to break the high of its first 30 minutes, the plan's second way in.

deeper.trap: The 30 minutes set this setup's trigger. Buying at 9:42 means buying inside the range, before the level even exists.

reasons: the key rests on one repo page (TRADE_PLANS.md)
house rule from the owner's rulings

questions.lesson_line: Check the holiday calendar every Sunday. A short week changes when your plans can act.
questions.simple: Three, because the market is shut on Thanksgiving Thursday and closes early on the Friday after.

5 sessions
3 sessions

questions.story: Thursday, Dec. 24, 2026. Your plan sells a stock if it closes under its trail line. You set your usual alert for 3:55 p.m.
questions.q: What's the problem with that alert?
choices: The close is at 1:00 p.m. that day
Nothing, it's a normal full session
The market is shut the whole day
The market opens late that day
questions.answer: The close is at 1:00 p.m. that day
questions.why: The close comes at 1:00 p.m. NYSE closes early on Thursday, Dec. 24, 2026. A 3:55 p.m. alert fires hours after the close you meant to act on. The next day, Christmas, the market is shut. Check the calendar for early closes, not just closed days.
questions.lesson_line: On an early-close day the close comes at 1:00 p.m. Move every close-based exit alert up.

wrong.Nothing, it's a normal full session: Not this one. NYSE lists Dec. 24, 2026 as an early close at 1:00 p.m.
wrong.The market is shut the whole day: That's Christmas Day, Friday, Dec. 25. The 24th trades, but only until 1:00 p.m.
wrong.The market opens late that day: The open is not what changes. NYSE lists Dec. 24, 2026 as an early close at 1:00 p.m. It's the close that moves.

questions.simple: The market closes early at 1:00 p.m. on Christmas Eve, so a 3:55 alert comes hours too late.

reasons: the key rests on one source (NYSE calendar)

questions.story: Your stock reports earnings after today's close. Your plan says be out before the report. You'll be in a meeting from 3:30 p.m. on.
questions.q: Which order best gets you out before the report?
choices: A market-on-close sell, sent early
A sell stop under today's low
A sell order after hours at 4:05
A limit sell at today's closing price
questions.why: A market-on-close sell, sent early. An on-close order asks to trade at today's closing price, before the after-close report lands. It must arrive by the exchange cutoff: 3:50 p.m. on NYSE, before 3:55 p.m. on Nasdaq. Nasdaq does not guarantee market-on-close orders. A stop may never trigger, and after hours you may sell into the news.
questions.lesson_line: Away at the close: a market-on-close order asks for the closing price, if it's in on time.

wrong.A sell stop under today's low: A stop only goes to work if the stock trades down to it. If it doesn't, you hold right through the report.
wrong.A sell order after hours at 4:05: This report lands after the close, and after-hours trading is thinner, with wider spreads. You could be selling into the news.
wrong.A limit sell at today's closing price: You can't know today's close ahead of time, so a plain limit order can't aim at it. Only an on-close order asks for the closing price.

questions.simple: Send a market-on-close sell before you leave, since it asks to trade at today's close, before the report.

deeper.trap: The trap is holding just this once. Our rule: no new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report. Hold through one only if the trade is up 5R. Below that, be out before the report. When you can't watch the close, the on-close order is how you get out.

reasons: the story's plan rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.story: Sunday, Dec. 6, 2026. You're mapping the week. The Fed meets Tuesday and Wednesday. CPI comes out Thursday at 8:30 a.m.
questions.q: What makes this Friday's 4:00 p.m. close unusual?
choices: The Russell indexes rebalance
Standard monthly options expire
The jobs report comes out
It's an early 1:00 p.m. close
questions.why: The Russell indexes rebalance. From 2026 they rebuild in June and December, and the December changes take effect after the close on Friday, Dec. 11, 2026. Index funds trade into that close. At June's rebalance, $219.9 billion traded in the closing moments on NYSE and $334.0 billion on Nasdaq. These are 2026 dates: check the Russell page each year.
questions.lesson_line: Check the index calendar on Sunday. A rebalance Friday can bring a giant close.

wrong.The jobs report comes out: That came out last Friday, Dec. 4, at 8:30 a.m. And it lands before the open, not at the close.
wrong.It's an early 1:00 p.m. close: NYSE's early closes this season are Nov. 27 and Dec. 24. This Friday runs the full day.
wrong.Standard monthly options expire: Standard monthly options expire on the third Friday. This is the second Friday of December.

questions.simple: The Russell indexes rebalance at that close, so index funds trade huge size into the 4:00 p.m. bell.

deeper.trap: The Fed and CPI make the noise this week, and we trade those days like any other. The close that stands out may be Friday's, on the Russell date.

reasons: the key rests on one source (FTSE Russell)

questions.story: Friday, June 26, 2026. Your small-cap stock prints its biggest volume bar in a year. Much of it came in the final print at 4:00 p.m. Price barely moved.
questions.q: What most likely explains that volume?
choices: Index funds rebalancing at close
Big buyers quietly loading up
A breakout pulling in many new buyers
Monthly options expiring that day
questions.why: Index funds rebalancing at the close. The June 2026 Russell changes took effect after the close on Friday, June 26. In the closing moments that day, $219.9 billion traded on NYSE and $334.0 billion on Nasdaq. Index-fund managers generally trade near the close to match their benchmark. So a giant closing print on that date is not proof of demand.
questions.lesson_line: Before you read a giant volume bar as demand, check the calendar for an index rebalance.

wrong.Big buyers quietly loading up: Maybe, but much of it came in one closing print on a reconstitution day. That points to index funds trading the close.
wrong.A breakout pulling in many new buyers: Price barely moved, so nothing broke out. The volume came in one print at the close, the way index rebalancing trades.
wrong.Monthly options expiring that day: Standard monthly options expire on the third Friday. June 26, 2026 was the fourth Friday, the Russell date.

questions.simple: Index funds rebalancing at the close most likely made that volume, since June 26 was the Russell date.

deeper.counter: A giant volume bar is not always demand. On an index rebalance day, funds trade the close to match their benchmark. Check the calendar before you read a volume record as buyers stepping in.

questions.story: Friday, 3:45 p.m. A stock on your list is trading back over its 4-day average of the highs, our Slingshot trigger. Fifteen minutes to the bell, then the weekend.
questions.q: What does our plan say to do?
choices: Buy as it trades through the trigger
Wait for the close to confirm it
Skip it, Fridays are bad to buy
Wait and buy Monday's open
questions.answer: Buy as it trades through the trigger
questions.why: Buy as it trades through the trigger. Every setup buys as price trades through its trigger, during the day. The stop goes under the low of day, the prior day's low, or the range low. Friday is not a reason to skip: no weekday has an edge on its own.
questions.lesson_line: The trigger is the entry, whenever it trades through. The close is not our entry.

wrong.Skip it, Fridays are bad to buy: That's folklore. The weekend effect weakened or disappeared once it was published, and no weekday has an edge on its own.
wrong.Wait and buy Monday's open: Monday's open is a different price, and weekend news can gap it far from your level. Our entry is the trigger.
wrong.Wait for the close to confirm it: Our entry is the trigger itself, as price trades through it. Waiting for the close is not the plan.

questions.simple: Buy as it trades through the trigger, because our setups enter on the trigger during the day, not at the close.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking the close makes the entry safer. Waiting for it can leave you well above the trigger, or out of the trade, and a higher entry means a wider stop. Our entry is the trigger itself.

reasons: the key rests on one repo page (TRADE_PLANS.md)

questions.q: A big buy imbalance at 3:50 p.m. locks in a close above the 3:50 price.
questions.why: False. Nothing locks in the close. The imbalance is published so others can bring orders that offset it. After 3:50 p.m., NYSE takes new market-on-close and limit-on-close orders only on the side opposite a significant imbalance. Nasdaq's imbalance-only orders exist to offset it, and Nasdaq does not guarantee market-on-close orders.
questions.lesson_line: An imbalance is information, not a promise. Offsetting orders can still move the closing price.
questions.simple: False, because the imbalance is shown so other traders can step in against it, and nothing locks in the close.

deeper.trap: A big buy imbalance is a fact about orders at 3:50, not a forecast of the close. Offsetting orders can still come in after it is shown. The auction price is set where the most shares pair off. Treat the imbalance as information, not a promise.

questions.story: A newsletter says the last session before a long weekend has averaged about five times a normal day's return. It says to buy before every holiday.
questions.q: Do you build your plan around it?
choices: No: it's small and may not last
Yes: five times normal is a real edge
Yes, and size up before each holiday
No: the numbers are likely made up
questions.answer: No: it's small and may not last
questions.why: No: it's small and may not last. Before long weekends the average day was +0.185%, against +0.033% on a normal day. That is about five times, but still fractions of a percent. The data call it statistically significant. For most retail traders, costs and spreads would likely erase the gain. And the pattern might not hold in the future.
questions.lesson_line: A calendar quirk measured in fractions of a percent is trivia, not a trading plan.

wrong.Yes: five times normal is a real edge: Five times a tiny number is still tiny. It's fractions of a percent, and costs can wipe it out.
wrong.Yes, and size up before each holiday: Sizing up on a quirk that costs can erase only adds risk.
wrong.No: the numbers are likely made up: The pattern shows up in real data, and it's statistically significant. The problem is its size and your costs, not fakery.

questions.simple: No, because the edge is a tiny fraction of a percent that costs can erase, and it may not last.

deeper.counter: A bigger average can still be a tiny number. Famous published anomalies, like the weekend effect, seem to have weakened or disappeared after they became known. A pattern everyone reads about is a weak base for a plan.

reasons: study numbers can change when the source updates

questions.story: At 9:34 a.m., a stock on your focus list hits its planned entry. The open is swinging hard today.
questions.q: What do our rules say to do?
choices: Buy now, with the stop and size set
Wait out the first half hour
Skip it, the open is too wild
Buy now, set stop once it calms
questions.answer: Buy now, with the stop and size set
questions.simple: Buy now, because our rulebook has no time-of-day rule and your written plan is the trigger.
questions.why: Buy now, with the stop and size set. Our rulebook has no time-of-day rule. Every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written before the open. The open tends to swing hardest, but the clock is not the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: We have no time-of-day rule. The planned entry decides, not the clock.

wrong.Wait out the first half hour: That's a time-of-day rule, and we don't have one. The planned entry is the trigger.
wrong.Skip it, the open is too wild: The open does tend to swing hardest. But we have no time-of-day rule, so the swing alone is no reason to skip.
wrong.Buy now, set stop once it calms: The stop doesn't wait. Our rule: every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens.

deeper.trap: The open's swings are a fact about the market, not a rule for you. Your entry, stop and size were written before the open. Act on them.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C30, D39)

conflicts: Spreads late in the day: McInish and Wood (NYSE stocks, Journal of Finance 1992) found a reverse-J shape, with spreads highest at the start of the day and turning up a little at the end; Cboe's 2020 study of S&P 500 names found spreads narrowing until the close, with a small rise at 3:50 p.m. Both agree spreads are widest at the open, and that is all q03, q04 and q11 key. No question says spreads are widest or narrowest at the close.

Independence of the volume-shape sources: Investopedia's intraday paragraph lists Schwab's 'Trading Near the Bells' among its article sources, so the two are not fully independent. q01 and q08 also cite Hong and Wang (2000), a Journal of Finance theory paper whose abstract lists 'higher trading activity around the close and open' and U-shaped volatility as empirical findings its model matches; q08 also cites Foster and Viswanathan (1993), which found volume and volatility higher in the first half hour in 1988 NYSE data. (Checker, 2026-11-09: corrected an earlier line here that said both papers used NYSE data; Hong and Wang is theory.)

Buying late in the day: Schwab's 'Trading Near the Bells' says the end of the day 'may not been seen as a great time to add a position', while several UCT setups (Slingshot, Launchpad, Gap Support, High Volume Edge) enter on the close (TRADE_PLANS.md). No question keys Schwab's view. Our close entries are asked as ours (q18, w2), and the unit never says late-day buying is better or worse in general.

On-close cutoffs differ by exchange: NYSE's auction fact sheet (2024) puts the MOC/LOC cutoff at 3:50 p.m.; Nasdaq's crosses FAQ (2025) takes market-on-close orders until 3:55 p.m. (limit-on-close until 3:58 p.m.). Brokers can set earlier cutoffs. q15 says 'sent early' and tells the member to check the broker's cutoff; q09 asks only what starts at 3:50 p.m. on both, which both documents agree on (NYSE: significant imbalance publication and the 3:50 to 4:00 p.m. closing imbalance period; Nasdaq: imbalance dissemination from 3:50 p.m.).

The long-weekend pattern (q20): Investopedia's own 2000-2024 S&P 500 analysis calls the pre-holiday return statistically significant over 196 long weekends (+0.185% vs +0.033% a day), and also says spreads and costs would likely erase the gain for most retail investors. Its general cost threshold (0.05% to 0.09% round trip for S&P 500 names) is below that 0.15% gap, so the key avoids 'too small to beat costs' as a flat fact and keys 'small and may not last', which rests on Investopedia's 'fractions of a percent' and Schwert's NBER finding that published calendar effects weakened or disappeared.

Time-sensitive facts read on 2026-11-09: NYSE 2026 holidays and early closes (Nov. 26 closed, Nov. 27 1:00 p.m., Dec. 24 1:00 p.m., Dec. 25 closed); the Russell move to semi-annual reconstitution from 2026, with the December 2026 changes effective after the close on Dec. 11; the FOMC's Dec. 8-9 meeting; BLS release dates (jobs Dec. 4, CPI Dec. 10). Nasdaq and NYSE Arca plan an overnight session from December 6, 2026 (see F1.05's conflicts); the regular session, its 9:30 a.m. and 4:00 p.m. auctions and the 3:50 p.m. imbalance events are not changed by it. Re-read the Russell page and the NYSE calendar after Dec. 11, 2026 before reusing q13, q14 or q16 as current-year questions.

Q2 2024 closing-auction share (f20) is a share of notional value across all US equities, from NYSE research; NYSE's April 2026 note gives a record 605.5 million NYSE closing-auction shares a day in Q1 2026 but no percent. No question states a percent of daily volume; q05 and w1 say only 'often one of the day's biggest trades'.

Checker, 2026-11-09: Schwab's 'Trading Near the Bells' also says higher volume 'leads to tighter bid-ask spreads', which a member could read as 'spreads are tight at the busy open'. The measured data disagree for the open: Cboe (S&P 500 names, 2020) finds spreads widest at the open and McInish and Wood (NYSE) a reverse J, highest at the start. The unit keys the measured data (q03, q04, q11) and never keys Schwab's general line.

Checker, 2026-11-09: after 3:50 p.m. NYSE limits new market-on-close and limit-on-close orders to the side that offsets a significant imbalance, but its September 2026 memo (RM-26-15) also says 'Closing IO Orders may be entered on both sides of the market up to 4:00 p.m.' (they execute only against an imbalance) and the Auctions page lets floor-broker D orders in until 3:59:50 p.m. So q09, q19 and w2 now say 'market-on-close and limit-on-close orders', not 'on-close orders' in general.
